topics.title: Chapter 16 — Bash Scripting for Administrators
topics.summary: A script is a program with administrative consequences. HarborWorks uses Bash for small compositions of existing tools, not as a reason to avoid design. The examples in this chapter emphasize input validation, exact path handling, meaningful failure, and repeatable outcomes.

topics.summary: Create a text file beginning with #!/usr/bin/env bash, followed by commands. Run it with bash script.sh during development; executable permission plus the interpreter line permits ./script.sh. A .sh suffix is a naming convention, not what makes the file executable.

Start with a harmless program that prints a message and the hostname. Run bash -n script.sh to check shell syntax before execution. This does not validate external commands, permissions, or runtime logic. For privileged deployment, use an approved interpreter path and trusted PATH rather than depending on arbitrary environment contents.
Linux example — 16.1
Create and validate a first Bash script.

lab=$(mktemp -d)
cat > "$lab/hello.sh" <<'BASH'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf 'Hello from %s\n' "$(hostname)"
BASH
bash -n "$lab/hello.sh" && bash "$lab/hello.sh"

topics.title: 16.4 Exit Codes
topics.summary: A command returns zero for its defined success and nonzero for other outcomes. Capture a status immediately if it is needed. grep is a classic distinction: one means no match, while a larger status indicates an error. Treating all nonzero statuses as the same can turn a missing file into an empty report.

A function should make its output contract clear. If it returns data through stdout, keep diagnostic messages on stderr so the caller does not parse a warning as a filename. Do not hide privileged mutations in a function whose name sounds observational, such as check_storage, unless its behavior is explicit.

Define and call a function.

report_path() { stat -c '%F %n' -- "$1"; }
report_path /etc/passwd

topics.title: 16.9 Input and Output
topics.summary: Standard input carries incoming data, stdout carries the main result, and stderr carries diagnostics. Redirect them deliberately. A report saved with command >report 2>errors separates results from problems, while 2>&1 combines streams at the point the redirection is evaluated.

blocks.text: set -e requests exit for certain unhandled failures, -u rejects many unset-variable expansions, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail when a component fails rather than considering only the last command. These settings catch mistakes, but they are not an exception system.

-e has important exceptions in tests, conditional lists, pipelines, and functions called in conditional contexts. Command substitutions also have nuanced inheritance behavior. Arithmetic expressions such as ((count++)) can return nonzero when their expression evaluates to zero. Use explicit checks for critical operations and test failure paths instead of assuming “strict mode” proves correctness. (R36)

blocks.text: A useful script log identifies the operation, target, outcome, and time without exposing secrets. Write diagnostic lines to stderr and use a stable format. If stdout is intended as machine-readable data, keep it free of decorative progress messages.

Do not enable set -x around secrets: tracing can reveal expanded arguments and assignments. Debug a sanitized fixture first. An administrator should be able to tell the difference between “nothing changed,” “change completed,” and “operation failed before any change.”

blocks.text: Keep scripts small enough to reason about. The companion includes a read-only host report, a bounded HTTP check, and a status-page renderer. Each has a narrow contract rather than a universal “configure my server” function.

Move to a more suitable language or configuration tool when you need complex data structures, robust structured parsing, concurrent transactions, or extensive cross-platform behavior. Bash is excellent glue when the interfaces are clear. It becomes fragile when every input is repeatedly converted into and out of shell syntax.

topics.title: 16.16 Writing Safe and Idempotent Scripts
topics.summary: An idempotent operation reaches the same intended state when repeated. It does not append another duplicate line or restart a healthy service without need. Compare the desired file with the existing file and replace only when content differs.

concepts.definition: An idempotent operation reaches the same intended state when repeated. It does not append another duplicate line or restart a healthy service without need. Compare the desired file with the existing file and replace only when content differs.

blocks.text: An idempotent operation reaches the same intended state when repeated. It does not append another duplicate line or restart a healthy service without need. Compare the desired file with the existing file and replace only when content differs.

Idempotence is not the same as safety or atomicity. Repeatedly deleting the wrong directory can be idempotent and disastrous. A safe script validates its target, limits privileges, reports errors, and respects concurrency assumptions. Tests should include unchanged input, invalid input, paths containing spaces, and an existing output that must survive failure.

topics.title: Requirement and simplest approach
topics.summary: Write index.html into an existing, trusted, user-owned lab directory. Accept only UP, DEGRADED, or DOWN. Invalid input must leave any existing page unchanged. Repeating the same state must not replace an identical file. There is one writer, and no untrusted user can alter the directory or its parents during execution.

blocks.text: Write index.html into an existing, trusted, user-owned lab directory. Accept only UP, DEGRADED, or DOWN. Invalid input must leave any existing page unchanged. Repeating the same state must not replace an identical file. There is one writer, and no untrusted user can alter the directory or its parents during execution.

Directly writing echo ... >index.html truncates the existing page before the replacement is complete. The selected design validates first, writes a same-directory temporary file, compares content, and renames only after successful generation. The complete companion script follows this mechanism:

#!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail if (( $# != 2 )); then printf 'Usage: %s OUTPUT_DIR STATE\n' "$0" >&2 exit 2 fi out_dir=$1 state=$2 case "$state" in UP|DEGRADED|DOWN) ;; *) printf 'Invalid state\n' >&2; exit 2 ;; esac if [[ ! -d "$out_dir" || -L "$out_dir" || ! -O "$out_dir" ]]; then printf 'Need a trusted directory owned by this user\n' >&2 exit 2 fi out_dir=$(cd -- "$out_dir" && pwd -P) target="$out_dir/index.html" if [[ -L "$target" || ( -e "$target" && ! -f "$target" ) ]]; then printf 'Refusing non-regular target\n' >&2 exit 2 fi tmp=$(mktemp "$out_dir/.harbor-status.XXXXXX") trap 'rm -f -- "$tmp"' EXIT printf '\n\n' >"$tmp" printf 'HarborStatus\n' >>"$tmp" printf '

HarborStatus

State: %s

\n\n' \ "$state" >>"$tmp" chmod 0644 "$tmp" if [[ -f "$target" ]]; then if cmp -s -- "$tmp" "$target"; then printf 'unchanged\n' exit 0 else rc=$? if (( rc != 1 )); then printf 'Comparison failed\n' >&2 exit "$rc" fi fi fi mv -fT -- "$tmp" "$target" printf 'updated\n'

labs.title: Publish complete validated content
labs.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
lab_dir=$(mktemp -d)
trap 'rm -rf -- "$lab_dir"' EXIT
cd -- "$lab_dir"
printf 'old\n' > status
printf 'new\n' > status.tmp
test "$(cat status)" = old
mv status.tmp status
test "$(cat status)" = new
printf 'old until replacement; new after replacement\n'
